title: Looking back: the daily banis
hook: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, heard in order

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurta Gaddi: in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and your line, the eternal guru. Did you bow, or simply pause, before a book of the Guru's words? Today we turn around and look back at the year. Day six hundred ninety-two.

Six banis. One day. Picture a Sikh home before dawn: a kettle, a dark window, a voice already reading. By breakfast, several prayers have passed. At dusk, another. At bedtime, one more, said with the lights low. This year you met each of those prayers on its own, block by block, sometimes for weeks at a time. Today, for once, you hear them the way they're actually lived: in order, one day long. Looking back: the daily banis.
screen: `SIX BANIS, ONE DAY.` → `MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.` → `HEARD IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Start in the dark. Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, is when many Sikhs rise, bathe and begin. After the Japji comes the Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise, all short lines and quick meters. You met its line in the spring: namastvam akaale, salutation to the One beyond time. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, ten verses under the heading by Your grace. The poet has seen monks, yogis and mighty kings by the thousand, and says all of it is worth nothing without love. Then, in many homes, the Benti Chaupai, a prayer for shelter: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, give me Your hand and keep me safe. And then Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, which opens with a cry of joy: anand bhaiaa meree maae, I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the morning. Then comes the day itself: work, traffic, dishes, people. The banis don't ask anyone to leave it. They frame it. At dusk, Rehras, provisions for the road as work ends. It opens with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits and cares for all. And last, at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns, beginning jai ghar keerat aakheeai: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung. The same hymns are sung at funerals, so the close of a day and the close of a life share one song. Notice what the order does. Praise first, before anything has happened. Shelter for the hours ahead. Joy. Food for the road. A song for sleep. The whole day, held between words.
screen: `AMRITVELA: JAAP AND THE SAVAIYE.` · `SHELTER AND BLISS: CHAUPAI, ANAND.` · `DUSK: REHRAS, PROVISIONS FOR THE ROAD.` · `NIGHT: SOHILA, THE SONG FOR SLEEP.` · then, large: `THE DAY, HELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line from each, six lines, one day. Sit comfortably. Say them slowly, aloud or under your breath, with a full breath between each. Namastvam akaale. Tav prasad, by Your grace. Hamree karo hath dai rachhaa. Anand bhaiaa meree maae. So dar. Jai ghar keerat aakheeai. If a line won't come, say it in English, and let that be enough. Then rest in the quiet that's left after the sixth. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Turning around near the top of the year to see the daily banis together: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, from before dawn to bedtime.
Your line: the day, held. Today, notice the two edges of your day, the first thing you do and the last, and give one of them a line. Day six hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs say the Japji, Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye in the early morning, often with Chaupai and Anand Sahib, then Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila before sleep.

match.prompt: the daily banis — tap the pairs.
pairs: salutation to the One beyond time
I am in bliss, O my mother

myth: Kirtan Sohila is only ever said at bedtime
it is also sung at funerals: the close of a day and of a life share one song.
Rehras is said at dusk, as the day's work ends
it's the evening prayer, like provisions for the night's road.
the Savaiye say outward power counts for much even without love
they say the opposite: monks, yogis and kings are worth nothing without love.

fork.setup: the work is done and the light is going. which bani do many Sikhs say now?
fork.reveal: Rehras is the dusk prayer; Jaap belongs to the morning, and Asa di Var is sung before sunrise.

original.note: Punjabi: the word of the Gurus, the hymns themselves; the daily banis are the ones said each day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the daily prayers are a checklist to get through.
what it means: they frame a whole day, praise at dawn, shelter, joy, provisions at dusk, a song for sleep.
what a scholar hears: the set mixes hymns of Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan with compositions Sikhs attribute to the Tenth Guru, and Kirtan Sohila doubles as the funeral hymn.

notes: The Sikh Rehat Maryada lists Japji, Jaap and the ten Savaiye for the morning; Chaupai and Anand are said in the morning 'in many homes' (and by many Amritdhari Sikhs as the five banis). Confirm wording.
Transliterated lines (namastvam akaale, hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, anand bhaiaa meree maae, so dar, jai ghar keerat aakheeai) follow the y2 outline; Keeper to confirm transliteration.

Jaap, Savaiye and Chaupai are attributed to Guru Gobind Singh by the Rehat Maryada and Sikh tradition; some academic scholars debate parts of Dasam Granth authorship. The trapdoor now says 'compositions Sikhs attribute to the Tenth Guru' (and adds Guru Ram Das, whose hymns are in Rehras and Sohila); Keeper to confirm whether the teach should keep the plain attribution.
Savaiye paraphrase combines verse 1 (monks, siddhas, yogis) and verse 2 (mighty kings); confirm.
